content: The World Health Organization (WHO) has developed comprehensive guidelines addressing mental health in the workplace, recognizing the significant interplay between mental health and work. Mental health is not merely the absence of mental health conditions but rather a state of well-being that enables individuals to manage life’s stresses, realize their potential, learn effectively, work productively, and contribute to their communities. Mental health conditions can arise regardless of whether work has directly contributed to them. Poor mental health negatively impacts cognitive, emotional, social, and physical well-being, as well as personal identity and functioning in the workplace. This can lead to reduced productivity, impaired performance, challenges in maintaining or obtaining employment, and difficulties in working safely. These issues also contribute to broader economic consequences, including presenteeism (working while unwell), absenteeism, and staff turnover. Globally, approximately 15% of working-age adults experience a mental health condition at any given time. Despite the significant public health burden posed by mental health conditions, investment in addressing these issues remains insufficient. This is concerning, given international conventions advocating for the protection of workers’ physical and mental health through national occupational safety and health policies. The WHO guidelines provide evidence-based recommendations to promote mental health and prevent mental health conditions in the workplace. These include organizational interventions, training for managers and workers, and individual-level strategies. The guidelines also address returning to work after an absence due to mental health conditions and supporting individuals with mental health conditions in gaining employment. The recommendations are tailored to different groups, including all workers (universal interventions), workers at risk of mental health conditions (selective interventions), and those experiencing emotional distress or mental health conditions (indicated interventions). Key recommendations include: 1. Manager Training: Managers, particularly those overseeing health, humanitarian, and emergency workers, should receive training to enhance their knowledge, attitudes, and behaviors regarding mental health. This training aims to improve their ability to support the mental well-being of their teams. 2. Worker Training: Health, humanitarian, and emergency workers should be trained in mental health literacy and awareness to improve their understanding of mental health issues and reduce stigmatizing attitudes in the workplace. 3. Universal Individual Interventions: Psychosocial interventions, such as mindfulness-based or cognitive-behavioral approaches, can help workers develop stress management skills, promote positive mental health, reduce emotional distress, and enhance work effectiveness. 4. Targeted Interventions for Health, Humanitarian, and Emergency Workers: Psychosocial interventions, including stress management, self-care training, and communication skills training, should be made available to workers experiencing emotional distress. These interventions aim to reduce symptoms and improve mental health outcomes. 5. Support for Workers with Emotional Distress: For workers experiencing emotional distress, interventions such as mindfulness-based or cognitive-behavioral approaches, problem-solving training, or physical exercise (e.g., aerobic or weight training) may help alleviate symptoms and improve work performance. 6. Returning to Work After Mental Health-Related Absence: For individuals returning to work after an absence due to mental health conditions, a combination of work-directed care and evidence-based clinical mental health care, or clinical care alone, should be considered. These approaches aim to reduce mental health symptoms and minimize the duration of work absences. The WHO anticipates that these guidelines will drive action at both national and workplace levels, influencing policy development, service planning, and delivery in the fields of mental and occupational health. By implementing these evidence-based interventions, workplaces can foster positive mental health, reduce the burden of mental health conditions, and enhance overall productivity and well-being.
